title: AlphaZero: Mastering Games from Scratch
hook: AlphaGo learned from human games. AlphaZero threw those away — one algorithm reached superhuman chess, shogi, and Go knowing only the rules and playing itself.
key_points: A single general algorithm masters chess, shogi, and Go to superhuman strength.
Learns entirely from self-play, with no human game data — only the rules of each game.
Pairs one neural network (predicting moves and outcomes) with Monte Carlo tree search.
Starting from random play, it surpassed strong existing programs in each game.
content_html: David Silver, Thomas Hubert, and the DeepMind team generalized their game-playing work into AlphaZero, a single algorithm that masters chess, shogi, and Go to superhuman strength. Unlike its predecessors, it uses no human games at all — just the rules — and learns purely by playing against itself from random beginnings. The same method, with no game-specific tuning, reached top-tier play in three very different games, showing how far self-play alone can go.
extra_html:
How it works

AlphaZero uses one neural network that, for a given position, predicts both which moves look good and who is likely to win. That network guides a Monte Carlo tree search, which looks ahead and produces stronger move choices than the raw network alone. Those improved choices become training targets, so the network gradually teaches itself. The loop starts from random play and bootstraps upward through millions of self-played games, with no human examples in the mix.

Why it matters

Removing human data was the headline: it showed that strong play could emerge from rules plus self-play, rather than from imitating people, and that the same recipe transfers across games. That generality made AlphaZero a landmark in reinforcement learning and a template for later self-improving systems. It also produced strikingly creative play in chess and Go that influenced how human experts think about those games.
